claim: RIG-I, LGP2, and MDA5 initiate an antiviral response that includes production of type I interferons (IFNs).
source: The RIG-I-like receptors RIG-I, LGP2, and MDA5 initiate an antiviral response that includes production of type I interferons (IFNs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of innate immunity, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: The nature of the RNAs that trigger MDA5 activation in infected cells remains unclear.
source: The nature of the RNAs that trigger MDA5 activation in infected cells remains unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge at the time of the study and sets up the research question.

claim: LGP2/RNA complexes from cells infected with EMCV contain RNA that is highly enriched for MDA5-stimulatory activity.
source: Here, we purify and characterise LGP2/RNA complexes from cells infected with encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV), a picornavirus detected by MDA5 and LGP2 but not RIG-I. We show that those complexes contain RNA that is highly enriched for MDA5-stimulatory activity and for a specific sequence corresponding to the L region of the EMCV antisense RNA.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental purification and characterization of LGP2/RNA complexes showing enrichment for MDA5-stimulatory activity.

claim: LGP2/RNA complexes from EMCV-infected cells are enriched for a specific sequence corresponding to the L region of the EMCV antisense RNA.
source: We show that those complexes contain RNA that is highly enriched for MDA5-stimulatory activity and for a specific sequence corresponding to the L region of the EMCV antisense RNA.
evidence: Deep sequencing data and RT-PCR analysis demonstrate enrichment of L region antisense RNA in LGP2 immunoprecipitates.

claim: In vitro transcription of the L region sequence is sufficient to generate an MDA5 stimulatory RNA.
source: Synthesis of this sequence by in vitro transcription is sufficient to generate an MDA5 stimulatory RNA.
evidence: Figure 4 shows that in vitro transcribed L antisense RNA stimulates MDA5-dependent IFN responses.

claim: Genomic deletion of the L region in EMCV generates viruses that are less potent at stimulating MDA5-dependent IFN production.
source: Conversely, genomic deletion of the L region in EMCV generates viruses that are less potent at stimulating MDA5-dependent IFN production.
evidence: Figures 5, 6, and 7 show reduced IFN stimulatory activity and reduced innate immune responses with EMCV ΔL mutants.

claim: The L region antisense RNA of EMCV is a key determinant of innate immunity to the virus.
source: Thus, the L region antisense RNA of EMCV is a key determinant of innate immunity to the virus and represents an RNA that activates MDA5 in virally-infected cells.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including deletion mutants, in vitro transcription, and in vivo infection studies support this conclusion.

claim: The L region antisense RNA represents an RNA that activates MDA5 in virally-infected cells.
source: Thus, the L region antisense RNA of EMCV is a key determinant of innate immunity to the virus and represents an RNA that activates MDA5 in virally-infected cells.
evidence: The combination of LGP2 pulldown enrichment, MDA5-dependent stimulation, and functional validation with mutant viruses supports this conclusion.

claim: Type I interferons (IFN-α/β) are produced in response to viral infection in mammals.
source: Viral infection in mammals triggers a rapid innate immune response involving the production of antiviral proteins and proinflammatory mediators, prominent among which are the type I interferons (IFN-α/β; hereafter, IFN) (Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006; Takaoka and Yanai, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IFNs induce the transcription of more than 300 IFN-stimulated genes.
source: IFNs are secreted cytokines that act on all nucleated cells to induce the transcription of more than 300 IFN-stimulated genes, whose products collectively limit virus replication and spread (Haller et al., 2007; Schoggins and Rice, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IFN gene transcription is triggered by the activation of pattern recognition receptors that detect viral invasion.
source: IFN gene transcription is triggered by the activation of pattern recognition receptors that detect viral invasion.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in innate immunity.

claim: The RLR family comprises three members: RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2.
source: The RLR family comprises three members: RIG-I (retinoic acid-induced gene I), MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5), and LGP2 (laboratory of genetics and physiology 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Binding of agonistic RNA by RIG-I or MDA5 triggers a signalling cascade that leads to the activation of transcription factors, including several of the IFN regulatory factors (IRFs).
source: Binding of agonistic RNA by RIG-I or MDA5 triggers a signalling cascade that leads to the activation of transcription factors, including several of the IFN regulatory factors (IRFs), which translocate into the nucleus to induce expression of IFN and other genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RLR signaling pathways.

claim: LGP2 lacks a signalling domain and cannot act in the same manner as RIG-I or MDA5.
source: LGP2 lacks a signalling domain and cannot act in the same manner.
evidence: This is based on the known structural features of LGP2.

claim: LGP2 is thought to potentiate MDA5-dependent IFN induction.
source: Rather, LGP2 is thought to potentiate MDA5-dependent IFN induction although the exact mechanism by which this occurs remains unclear (Satoh et al., 2010; Bruns et al., 2012; Childs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MDA5 and RIG-I are activated by different RNA viruses.
source: MDA5 and RIG-I are activated by different RNA viruses (Kato et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RIG-I is non-redundant for detection of influenza or Sendai virus but dispensable for responses to picornaviruses.
source: RIG-I is non-redundant for detection of influenza or Sendai virus but dispensable for responses to picornaviruses whereas the opposite is the case for MDA5 (Kato et al., 2006; 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MDA5 is non-redundant for detection of picornaviruses but dispensable for responses to influenza or Sendai virus.
source: RIG-I is non-redundant for detection of influenza or Sendai virus but dispensable for responses to picornaviruses whereas the opposite is the case for MDA5 (Kato et al., 2006; 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RIG-I binds to and is activated by base-paired RNA containing a 5′ triphosphate extremity.
source: RIG-I binds to and is activated by base-paired RNA containing a 5′ triphosphate extremity (Hornung et al., 2006; Pichlmair et al., 2006; Schlee et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009) as found in influenza and Sendai virus genomes (Baum et al., 2010; Rehwinkel et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MDA5 recognizes RNA independently of 5′ phosphates.
source: In contrast, MDA5 recognizes RNA independently of 5′ phosphates and can be activated in cells by transfection of synthetic poly I:C or the double-stranded (ds) RNA genome segments of reovirus (Kato et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MDA5 can be activated in cells by transfection of synthetic poly I:C or the double-stranded (ds) RNA genome segments of reovirus.
source: In contrast, MDA5 recognizes RNA independently of 5′ phosphates and can be activated in cells by transfection of synthetic poly I:C or the double-stranded (ds) RNA genome segments of reovirus (Kato et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It has been concluded that MDA5 detects long dsRNA generated during virus infection.
source: Based on such observations, it has been concluded that MDA5 detects long dsRNA generated during virus infection.
evidence: This represents a prevailing interpretation in the field based on prior observations.

claim: Natural MDA5 agonists derived from infected cells remain poorly characterised.
source: However, natural MDA5 agonists derived from infected cells remain poorly characterised.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge and justifies the current study.

claim: Some studies have suggested that MDA5 agonists might correspond to high molecular weight RNA complexes containing double and single-stranded (ss) regions.
source: Some studies have suggested that they might correspond to high molecular weight RNA complexes containing double and single-stranded (ss) regions (Pichlmair et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Other reports have proposed that relevant MDA5 agonists are specific viral replication intermediates.
source: Other reports have proposed that relevant MDA5 agonists are specific viral replication intermediates (Feng et al., 2012; Triantafilou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It has been suggested that MDA5 might also be activated by RNA products of RNAseL cleavage.
source: Finally, it has been suggested that MDA5 might also be activated by RNA products of RNAseL cleavage (Malathi et al., 2010; Luthra et al., 2011) or by mRNA bearing unmethylated cap structures (Züst et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It has been suggested that MDA5 might be activated by mRNA bearing unmethylated cap structures.
source: Finally, it has been suggested that MDA5 might also be activated by RNA products of RNAseL cleavage (Malathi et al., 2010; Luthra et al., 2011) or by mRNA bearing unmethylated cap structures (Züst et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of RIG-I from cells infected with influenza A virus (IAV) or Sendai virus has allowed the identification of physiological RIG-I agonists.
source: Immunoprecipitation of RIG-I from cells infected with influenza A virus (IAV) or Sendai virus has allowed the identification of physiological RIG-I agonists (Baum et al., 2010; Rehwinkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EMCV is a member of the Cardiovirus genus of picornaviruses.
source: In this study, we use an analogous approach to investigate the nature of MDA5 agonists in cells infected with encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV), a member of the Cardiovirus genus of picornaviruses.
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification of the virus.

claim: Picornaviruses are single-stranded positive-strand (sense) RNA viruses that replicate in infected cells via a negative-strand (antisense) intermediate.
source: Picornaviruses are single-stranded positive-strand (sense) RNA viruses that replicate in infected cells via a negative-strand (antisense) intermediate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about picornavirus replication.

claim: RNA purified from LGP2 immunoprecipitation complexes is enriched for MDA5 stimulatory RNA corresponding to a portion of the EMCV antisense RNA.
source: We purify RNA directly from complexes obtained by immunoprecipitation of LGP2 and show that this method enriches for MDA5 stimulatory RNA corresponding to a portion of the EMCV antisense RNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combination of functional assays and sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of the L region from EMCV generates viruses that produce less stimulatory RNA.
source: Deletion of the region encoding this antisense RNA generates viruses that produce less stimulatory RNA and are less potent at inducing IFN in infected cells or mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with EMCV deletion mutants shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: EMCV deletion mutants lacking the L region are less potent at inducing IFN in infected cells or mice.
source: Deletion of the region encoding this antisense RNA generates viruses that produce less stimulatory RNA and are less potent at inducing IFN in infected cells or mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: A discrete region of the EMCV negative-strand RNA acts as a physiologically-relevant MDA5 agonist in infected cells.
source: Thus, a discrete region of the EMCV negative-strand RNA acts as a physiologically-relevant MDA5 agonist in infected cells.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by multiple lines of evidence including LGP2 pulldown, sequencing, functional assays with mutant viruses, and in vivo experiments.

claim: Both MDA5 and LGP2 are required for IFN responses to EMCV.
source: To confirm that both MDA5 and LGP2 are required for IFN responses to EMCV (Kato et al., 2006; Satoh et al., 2010), we used mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) carrying null mutant alleles of the genes Ifih1 and Dhx58 encoding MDA5 and LGP2, respectively.
evidence: This is confirmed by experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by prior citations.

claim: The upregulation of Ifit1 or Ifnb1 mRNA was greatly impaired in MDA5- or LGP2-deficient MEFs infected with EMCV.
source: The upregulation of Ifit1 or Ifnb1 mRNA was greatly impaired in MDA5- or LGP2-deficient MEFs infected with EMCV (Figure1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: MDA5- or LGP2-deficient MEFs responded normally to RIG-I-dependent viruses such as IAV and to known RIG-I agonists such as in vitro transcribed (IVT) RNA.
source: The same cells responded normally to RIG-I-dependent viruses such as IAV and to known RIG-I agonists such as in vitro transcribed (IVT) RNA (Figure1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: EMCV genomes extracted from purified viral particles did not stimulate the IFN-β reporter.
source: As seen in Figure 1A, EMCV genomes did not stimulate the IFN-β reporter, in contrast to the genomes of IAV, which directly activate RIG-I (Baum et al., 2010; Rehwinkel et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IAV genomes directly activate RIG-I.
source: As seen in Figure 1A, EMCV genomes did not stimulate the IFN-β reporter, in contrast to the genomes of IAV, which directly activate RIG-I (Baum et al., 2010; Rehwinkel et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 1A.

claim: RNA isolated from cells in which EMCV viral replication had been permitted potently induced the IFN-β reporter upon transfection into HEK293 cells.
source: RNA isolated from cells in which EMCV viral replication had been permitted to take its course (DMSO control) potently induced the IFN-β reporter upon transfection into HEK293 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNA extracted from HeLa cells treated with ribavirin during EMCV infection was non-stimulatory.
source: In contrast, RNA extracted from HeLa cells treated with ribavirin was non-stimulatory (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment of the reporter HEK293 cells with ribavirin did not affect the response to EMCV RNA.
source: Treatment of the reporter HEK293 cells themselves with ribavirin did not affect the response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), which indicates that the stimulatory RNA is preformed in EMCV-infected HeLa cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The stimulatory RNA is preformed in EMCV-infected HeLa cells.
source: Treatment of the reporter HEK293 cells themselves with ribavirin did not affect the response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), which indicates that the stimulatory RNA is preformed in EMCV-infected HeLa cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ribavirin treatment of reporter cells does not affect their response.

claim: The response in the HEK293 reporter cells to EMCV RNA was dependent on MDA5.
source: Furthermore, the response in the HEK293 reporter cells was dependent on MDA5 as demonstrated using RNA interference-mediated MDA5 knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: MDA5 and LGP2 activation results exclusively from RNA generated during active EMCV replication.
source: Altogether these data indicate that MDA5 and LGP2 activation results exclusively from RNA generated during active EMCV replication, as recently suggested (Feng et al., 2012; Triantafilou et al., 2012).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that ribavirin treatment abolishes stimulatory activity, supported by prior citations.

claim: The ssRNA but not the long dsRNA fraction extracted from cells infected with IAV stimulated the IFN reporter.
source: As expected (Pichlmair et al., 2006), the ssRNA but not the long dsRNA fraction extracted from cells infected with IAV, stimulated the IFN reporter (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Both ds and ssRNA fractions from cells infected with EMCV triggered the IFN-β reporter.
source: In contrast, both ds and ssRNA fractions from cells infected with EMCV triggered the IFN-β reporter (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Treatment of total RNA from EMCV-infected cells with RNase A or RNase III strongly reduced stimulatory activity.
source: Similarly, treatment of total RNA from EMCV-infected cells with RNase A or RNase III, which digest unpaired or base-paired RNA, respectively, strongly reduced stimulatory activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Removal of 5′ phosphates by digestion with calf intestinal phosphatase (CIP) or 5′ polyphophatase (PP) did not impact stimulatory activity of EMCV RNA.
source: In contrast, removal of 5′ phosphates by digestion with calf intestinal phosphatase (CIP) or 5′ polyphophatase (PP) did not impact stimulatory activity although it abrogated that of IVT control RNA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MDA5/LGP2 stimulatory RNA accumulates in EMCV-infected cells during virus replication and contains both ssRNA and dsRNA features.
source: Altogether these data indicate that MDA5/LGP2 stimulatory RNA accumulates in EMCV-infected cells during virus replication and contains both ssRNA and dsRNA features, as previously suggested (Pichlmair et al., 2009).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data from RNA fractionation and enzyme digestion experiments, supported by prior citation.

claim: RNA associated with the LGP2 precipitates, but not with control precipitates, stimulated the IFN-β luciferase reporter in HEK293 cells.
source: Notably, RNA associated with the LGP2 precipitates, but not with control (ctrl) precipitates, stimulated the IFN-β luciferase reporter in HEK293 cells and induced expression of the IFNB1 gene in HeLa cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: RNA associated with LGP2 precipitates induced expression of the IFNB1 gene in HeLa cells.
source: Notably, RNA associated with the LGP2 precipitates, but not with control (ctrl) precipitates, stimulated the IFN-β luciferase reporter in HEK293 cells and induced expression of the IFNB1 gene in HeLa cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Stimulatory activity was significantly enriched in the LGP2-immunoprecipitate when compared to input material.
source: Moreover, when compared to input material, stimulatory activity was significantly enriched in the LGP2-immunoprecipitate and was selectively depleted from the unbound fraction (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Stimulatory activity was selectively depleted from the unbound fraction after LGP2 immunoprecipitation.
source: Moreover, when compared to input material, stimulatory activity was significantly enriched in the LGP2-immunoprecipitate and was selectively depleted from the unbound fraction (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: LGP2-associated RNA isolated from immunoprecipitates stimulated IFN production in wild-type MEFs but not in LGP2- or MDA5-deficient MEFs.
source: Importantly, activity was lost in LGP2- or MDA5-deficient MEFs (Figure 2D), indicating that the LGP2-associated RNA isolated from immunoprecipitates is a pure MDA5/LGP2 agonist.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The LGP2-associated RNA isolated from immunoprecipitates is a pure MDA5/LGP2 agonist.
source: Importantly, activity was lost in LGP2- or MDA5-deficient MEFs (Figure 2D), indicating that the LGP2-associated RNA isolated from immunoprecipitates is a pure MDA5/LGP2 agonist.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that activity is lost in both LGP2- and MDA5-deficient MEFs.

claim: The IFN stimulatory capacity of LGP2-associated RNA was unaffected by treatment with CIP.
source: Consistent with this notion, its IFN stimulatory capacity was unaffected by treatment with CIP, which inactivates most RIG-I agonists, or Terminator (Term), which digests RNA with 5′ monophosphates (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The IFN stimulatory capacity of LGP2-associated RNA was unaffected by treatment with Terminator.
source: Consistent with this notion, its IFN stimulatory capacity was unaffected by treatment with CIP, which inactivates most RIG-I agonists, or Terminator (Term), which digests RNA with 5′ monophosphates (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Digestion of LGP2-associated RNA with RNaseT1 and RNaseIII completely abolished stimulatory potential.
source: Furthermore, digestion with RNaseT1 and RNaseIII completely abolished stimulatory potential (Figure 2E), again suggesting the presence of unpaired and base-paired RNA regions as previously observed with total RNA from EMCV-infected cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FLAG immunoprecipitation of recombinant LGP2 incubated with purified RNA from EMCV-infected HeLa cells allowed enrichment for stimulatory activity.
source: Finally, we incubated purified RNA from EMCV-infected HeLa cells together with recombinant FLAG-tagged LGP2 (Figure 2F). FLAG immunoprecipitation allowed enrichment for stimulatory activity when compared to a control IP, demonstrating that stimulatory RNA can associate with LGP2 in vitro in the absence of additional proteins (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Stimulatory RNA can associate with LGP2 in vitro in the absence of additional proteins.
source: FLAG immunoprecipitation allowed enrichment for stimulatory activity when compared to a control IP, demonstrating that stimulatory RNA can associate with LGP2 in vitro in the absence of additional proteins (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro reconstitution experiment shown in Figure 2F.

claim: LGP2 selectively associates with a pool of MDA5 agonists in EMCV-infected cells.
source: Altogether these results indicate that LGP2 selectively associates with a pool of MDA5 agonists in EMCV-infected cells and that LGP2 IP is a suitable approach to enrich for such agonists.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of the LGP2 immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: LGP2 IP is a suitable approach to enrich for MDA5 agonists.
source: Altogether these results indicate that LGP2 selectively associates with a pool of MDA5 agonists in EMCV-infected cells and that LGP2 IP is a suitable approach to enrich for such agonists.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of the LGP2 immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: The total number of reads mapping to EMCV represented around 30% in LGP2 IP samples vs only 4% and 6% in ctrl IP and input, respectively.
source: The total number of reads mapping to EMCV represented around 30% in LGP2 IP samples vs only 4% and 6% in ctrl IP and input, respectively (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 3A), which indicated that the RNA in the LGP2 IP is specifically enriched for EMCV-derived sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data shown in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: The RNA in the LGP2 IP is specifically enriched for EMCV-derived sequences.
source: The total number of reads mapping to EMCV represented around 30% in LGP2 IP samples vs only 4% and 6% in ctrl IP and input, respectively (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 3A), which indicated that the RNA in the LGP2 IP is specifically enriched for EMCV-derived sequences.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the sequencing data shown in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: The distribution of sequences in the LGP2 IP sample was not uniform but displayed a number of discrete peaks concentrated in the 5′ region of the EMCV genome.
source: Surprisingly, the distribution of sequences in the LGP2 IP sample was not uniform but displayed a number of discrete peaks concentrated in the 5′ region of the EMCV genome.
evidence: This is observed in the sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: One peak from position 735 nts to 905 nts on the antisense RNA was strongly enriched (25,000 reads/million) over input and ctrl IP samples.
source: In particular, one peak from position 735 nts to 905 nts on the antisense RNA was strongly enriched (25,000 reads/million) over input and ctrl IP samples (non detectable and 60 reads/million, respectively) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A smaller peak (±5,000 reads/million) in the corresponding part of the sense strand was also enriched in LGP2 IP samples.
source: A smaller peak (±5,000 reads/million) in the corresponding part of the sense strand was also enriched in LGP2 IP samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The enriched region encodes the leader (L) protein of EMCV.
source: This region encodes the leader (L) protein of EMCV and is henceforth referred to as the L region.
evidence: This is based on the genomic annotation of EMCV.

claim: Strand-specific RT-PCR confirmed that the L antisense but not the VP1 antisense region was enriched in LGP2 IP samples compared to ctrl IPs and input material.
source: To validate these findings, we used strand-specific RT-PCR with primers for the L antisense or, as a control, the VP1 antisense regions (primer localisation indicated by red arrows on the schematic representation of the EMCV genome in Figure 3B). This analysis confirmed that the L antisense but not the VP1 antisense region, was enriched in LGP2 IP samples compared to ctrl IPs and input material (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RNA that binds to LGP2 in vitro is enriched for the L antisense region.
source: These findings were further validated in the LGP2 in vitro reconstitution assay, which confirmed that RNA that binds to LGP2 is enriched for the L antisense region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro reconstitution data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: LGP2 association with EMCV RNA is strongly biased towards a discrete area of the negative (antisense) strand of the L protein-encoding region.
source: In sum, LGP2 association with EMCV RNA is strongly biased towards a discrete area of the negative (antisense) strand of the L protein-encoding region.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined sequencing and RT-PCR data.

claim: The RNA containing the L AS derived sequence was stimulatory in contrast to the one derived from the L sense sequence.
source: The RNA containing the L AS derived sequence was clearly stimulatory in contrast to the one derived from the L sense sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The activity of the CIP-treated L AS RNA was greatly reduced in MDA5-deficient but not RIG-I-deficient MEFs.
source: Moreover, the activity of the CIP-treated L AS was greatly reduced in the MDA5-deficient but not RIG-I-deficient MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: An IVT RNA corresponding to the EMCV L AS RNA sequence can trigger an MDA5-dependent IFN response.
source: We conclude that an IVT RNA corresponding to the EMCV L AS RNA sequence found in LGP2 immunoprecipitates (Figure 3) can trigger an MDA5-dependent IFN response.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: EMCV ΔLac, ΔLzn and ΔL are mutant viruses with partial or complete deletions of the L region.
source: To ask whether the L region of the EMCV genome is important for the generation of IFN stimulatory RNA, we used mutant EMCV viruses with partial (EMCV ΔLac and EMCV ΔLzn) or complete (EMCVΔL) deletions of that region (Dvorak et al., 2001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A, with citation to prior work.

claim: All three deletion mutant viruses (ΔLac, ΔLzn, ΔL) are attenuated due to the absence of the L protein.
source: Because all three viruses are attenuated due to the absence of the L protein, a known antagonist of IFN induction (Hato et al., 2007), we also amplified the Vp1 region to verify that similar levels of EMCV RNA were present in all samples (Figure 5B, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior work and verified by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The L protein is a known antagonist of IFN induction.
source: Because all three viruses are attenuated due to the absence of the L protein, a known antagonist of IFN induction (Hato et al., 2007), we also amplified the Vp1 region to verify that similar levels of EMCV RNA were present in all samples (Figure 5B, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RNA extracted from HeLa cells infected with EMCV ΔLac, ΔLzn or ΔL was slightly less stimulatory than RNA extracted from cells infected with wild-type EMCV.
source: In all cases, RNA extracted from HeLa cells infected with EMCV ΔLac, ΔLzn or ΔL was slightly less stimulatory than RNA extracted from cells infected with wild-type (WT) EMCV (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only a low amount of stimulatory RNA was recovered from LGP2 IPs following infection with the mutant viruses in contrast to infection with WT EMCV.
source: More importantly, only a low amount of stimulatory RNA was recovered from LGP2 IPs following infection with the mutant viruses in contrast to infection with WT EMCV (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The major species of stimulatory RNA associating with LGP2 in EMCV-infected cells derives from the L antisense region.
source: These results are consistent with the earlier indications that the major species of stimulatory RNA associating with LGP2 in EMCV-infected cells derives from the L antisense region.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that deletion of the L region reduces LGP2-associated stimulatory RNA.

claim: EMCV ZnC19AC22A carries two mutations in the zinc domain of the L protein, which inactivate function.
source: This virus carries two mutations in the zinc domain of the L protein, which inactivate function (Hato et al., 2007) but should not impact on the production of L RNA (even if that RNA now carries two nucleotide substitutions).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior research.

claim: The amount of stimulatory RNA in total cell extracts or associated with LGP2 precipitates was comparable upon infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A and EMCV WT.
source: Reassuringly, the amount of stimulatory RNA in total cell extracts (Figure 5E) or associated with LGP2 precipitates (Figure 5F) was comparable upon infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A and EMCV WT even though, as before, it was markedly reduced after EMCVΔL infection (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The lack of stimulatory LGP2-associated RNA observed after infection with EMCVΔL is specifically due to the loss of L region RNA rather than the loss of L protein function.
source: We conclude that the lack of stimulatory LGP2-associated RNA observed after infection with EMCVΔL is specifically due to the loss of L region RNA rather than the loss of L protein function.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison between EMCV ZnC19AC22A (which lacks L protein function but retains L RNA) and EMCVΔL (which lacks both).

claim: Upon infection with WT EMCV, induction of Ifit1 and Ifnb1 was limited in IFNAR1 KO BM-DCs.
source: Upon infection with WT EMCV, induction of Ifit1 and Ifnb1 was limited (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Induction of Ifit1 and Ifnb1 was markedly greater in response to infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A than with WT EMCV.
source: It was markedly greater in response to infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A, which encodes the non-functional mutant L protein (Figure 6A,B), consistent with the fact that the L protein inhibits IFN induction (Hato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6A,B and is consistent with prior knowledge about L protein function.

claim: Infection with EMCVΔL lacking both L protein and EMCV L region RNA induced lower levels of Ifnb1 or Ifit1 than infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A.
source: In contrast, infection with EMCVΔL lacking both L protein and EMCV L region RNA induced lower levels of Ifnb1 or Ifit1 than infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A at two different multiplicities of infection (MOI) (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: EMCV ΔL and EMCV ZnC19AC22A replicated to similar levels.
source: EMCV ΔL and EMCV ZnC19AC22A replicated to similar levels, indicating that any differences in stimulation by these viruses are not caused by variations in viral RNA levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The L region RNA of EMCV is important for RLR stimulation and viral restriction in infected cells.
source: These data show that the L region RNA of EMCV is important for RLR stimulation and viral restriction in infected cells and that this is independent on its ability to encode a functional L protein.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison of EMCV ZnC19AC22A and EMCVΔL.

claim: The importance of L region RNA for RLR stimulation is independent of its ability to encode a functional L protein.
source: These data show that the L region RNA of EMCV is important for RLR stimulation and viral restriction in infected cells and that this is independent on its ability to encode a functional L protein.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison of EMCV ZnC19AC22A (non-functional L protein) and EMCVΔL (no L region).

claim: The induction of both Ifit1 and Ifnb1 in response to EMCV LFMDV was comparable to that induced by EMCVΔL.
source: Notably, the induction of both Ifit1 and Ifnb1 in response to EMCV LFMDV was comparable to that induced by EMCVΔL (Figure 6A,B) and replication of the two strains was indistinguishable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The EMCV L AS RNA sequence rather than the position of the L region in the EMCV genome is the key determinant in innate stimulation.
source: These data suggest that the EMCV L AS RNA sequence rather than the position of the L region in the EMCV genome is the key determinant in innate stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that replacing the EMCV L region with the FMDV L region reduces stimulation.

claim: The chimeric influenza NS RNA containing the EMCV L antisense sequence remained dependent on RIG-I and not MDA5 for its stimulatory activity.
source: However, as shown in Figure 6D,E, the resulting chimeric NS RNA remained dependent on RIG-I and not MDA5 for its stimulatory activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: The L region antisense sequence needs to be somehow processed or released in the context of EMCV infection to trigger an MDA5-dependent response.
source: This suggests that the L region antisense sequence needs to be somehow processed or released in the context of EMCV infection to trigger an MDA5-dependent response and this does not happen in the context of the influenza virus NS segment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the L sequence in the influenza NS context does not activate MDA5.

claim: Higher levels of IFN-α were found in the serum of mice 24 hr after infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A when compared to EMCVΔL and WT.
source: Higher levels of IFN-α were found in the serum of mice 24 hr after infection with EMCV ZnC19AC22A when compared to EMCVΔL and WT (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vivo data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression of Ifit1 and Ifnb1 was much higher in hearts from mice infected with EMCV ZnC19AC22A compared to mice infected with EMCVΔL and WT.
source: In addition, the expression of Ifit1 and Ifnb1 was also much higher in hearts from mice infected with EMCV ZnC19AC22A compared to mice infected with EMCVΔL and WT (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vivo data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The presence of L region RNA independently of the function of the L protein is important for innate immune responses to EMCV infection in vivo.
source: We conclude that the presence of L region RNA independently of the function of the L protein is important for innate immune responses to EMCV infection in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the in vivo infection data comparing EMCV ZnC19AC22A and EMCVΔL.

claim: Pulldown of LGP2 allows isolation of MDA5 stimulatory RNA.
source: The finding that pulldown of LGP2 allows isolation of MDA5 stimulatory RNA is in agreement with the fact that both RLRs are required for IFN production upon EMCV infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and with previous reports describing LGP2 as a positive regulator of MDA5 signalling (Venkataraman et al., 2007; Satoh et al., 2010; Bruns et al., 2012; Childs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: LGP2 possesses higher avidity for RNA than MDA5.
source: One explanation may be that LGP2 possesses higher avidity for RNA than MDA5 (Bruns et al., 2012; Childs et al., 2013) and is therefore more prone to retain bound agonist during cell lysis and precipitation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and offered as a possible explanation for the success of LGP2 pulldown.

claim: MDA5 forms filaments along RNA upon activation.
source: Another possibility relates to the fact that MDA5 forms filaments along RNA upon activation (Peisley et al., 2011, 2012; Berke and Modis, 2012; Berke et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012) and that such structures—when formed in infected cells—may be difficult to isolate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LGP2 pulldown both enriches for MDA5 agonists and depletes them from input material.
source: Furthermore, we find that LGP2 pulldown both enriches for MDA5 agonists and depletes them from input material.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The universe of LGP2-bound RNAs largely overlaps with that of MDA5 agonists in EMCV-infected cells.
source: Therefore, it appears that the universe of LGP2-bound RNAs largely overlaps with that of MDA5 agonists in EMCV-infected cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment and depletion data.

claim: LGP2 may pre-select RNAs for MDA5 activation prior to the formation of MDA5 filaments.
source: Although we do not exclude the possibility that there are MDA5 agonists that are not captured by LGP2 pulldown (see below), our findings suggest a model where LGP2 pre-selects RNAs for MDA5 activation prior to the formation of MDA5 filaments.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: No specific enrichment for any human sequences was identified in LGP2-associated RNA by deep sequencing.
source: We were not able to identify specific enrichment for any human sequences (data not shown), a finding that does not support a dominant role for RNAseL cleaved self RNA in MDA5 activation (Malathi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on the sequencing analysis.

claim: The sequencing data do not support a dominant role for RNAseL cleaved self RNA in MDA5 activation during EMCV infection.
source: We were not able to identify specific enrichment for any human sequences (data not shown), a finding that does not support a dominant role for RNAseL cleaved self RNA in MDA5 activation (Malathi et al., 2007). This is in agreement with another recent publication that also failed to detect a significant role for RNaseL activity in EMCV-dependent IFN induction (Feng et al., 2012).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the sequencing data and is supported by citation to another study.

claim: The LGP2-associated RNA fragment is 171 nucleotides in length and corresponds to the antisense RNA in the L region of the genome.
source: This is a fragment of 171 nucleotides that corresponds to the antisense RNA in the L region of the genome.
evidence: This is determined from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: The short length of the LGP2-associated RNA and failure to be accompanied by the complementary strand are at odds with the notion that MDA5 is activated by long dsRNA.
source: Its short length and failure to be accompanied by the complementary strand are at odds with the notion that MDA5 is activated by long dsRNA (Kato et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data compared to prior understanding.

claim: MDA5 can form filaments along short dsRNA of around 100 nucleotides in length.
source: However, recent data indicate that MDA5 can form filaments along short dsRNA of around 100 nucleotides in length (Peisley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The LGP2-associated RNA appears to be single-stranded based on its sensitivity to ssRNA-specific RNases.
source: Moreover, the fact that LGP2-associated RNA appears to be single-stranded is in agreement with the observation that the stimulatory activity of the LGP2-associated RNA is sensitive to RNases that degrade ssRNA (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNase sensitivity data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The LGP2-associated RNA is sensitive to dsRNase treatment, suggesting the presence of base-paired regions important for MDA5/LGP2 recognition.
source: Interestingly, this LGP2-associated RNA is also sensitive to dsRNase treatment, which suggests the presence of base-paired regions important for MDA5/LGP2 recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNase sensitivity data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Heat denaturation destroyed the stimulatory activity of LGP2-associated RNA.
source: Consistent with that notion, heat denaturation destroyed its activity (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation.

claim: In silico analysis reveals the potential of the L antisense RNA to form hairpins.
source: In silico analysis reveals the potential of the L antisense RNA to form hairpins (data not shown), and such secondary and tertiary structure features may help to efficiently trigger MDA5 activation.
evidence: This is stated based on computational analysis.

claim: By in vitro transcription of a sequence corresponding to the L antisense region, an RNA that triggers MDA5 activation was created de novo.
source: Interestingly, by in vitro transcription of a sequence corresponding to the L antisense region we have succeeded in creating de novo an RNA that triggers MDA5 activation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Northern blots of RNA from EMCV-infected cells screened with an L AS sequence probe reveal many fragments smaller than the EMCV genome ranging between 200 and 2000 nucleotides.
source: However, Northern blots of RNA from EMCV-infected cells screened with an L AS sequence probe reveal many fragments smaller than the EMCV genome ranging between 200 and 2000 nucleotides (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observation.

claim: A previous study has reported the generation of a short subgenomic RNA fragment derived from the degradation of the non-polyadenylated genome of flaviviruses by the exonuclease XRN1.
source: Moreover, a previous study has reported the generation of a short subgenomic RNA fragment derived from the degradation of the non-polyadenylated genome of flaviviruses by the exonuclease XRN1 (Funk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is possible that a similar mechanism to XRN1 degradation could generate an L antisense RNA fragment.
source: It is possible that a similar mechanism could generate an L antisense RNA fragment.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to flavivirus RNA processing.

claim: Stress granule formation could potentially lead to degradation of viral RNA and generate the L region antisense RNA agonist.
source: Alternatively, stress granule formation, known to interfere with picornavirus replication (Borghese and Michiels, 2011), could potentially lead to degradation of viral RNA and generate the L region antisense RNA agonist.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior research on stress granules.

claim: MDA5 and LGP2 have been shown to associate with stress granules.
source: Interestingly, MDA5 and LGP2 have been recently shown to associate with stress granules (Onomoto et al., 2012; Langereis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recent study showed that negative-strand RNA synthesis is absolutely required for IFN induction during infection of mengovirus, a strain of EMCV.
source: A recent study showed that negative-strand RNA synthesis is absolutely required for IFN induction during infection of mengovirus, a strain of EMCV (Feng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The finding that a small RNA derived from the negative-strand RNA of EMCV associates with LGP2 and activates MDA5 is in line with the report that negative-strand RNA synthesis is required for IFN induction.
source: Our results that a small RNA derived from the negative-strand RNA of EMCV associates with LGP2 and activates MDA5 is in line with that report.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior research.

claim: Both the RF and RI forms can activate MDA5 upon transfection.
source: However, it has also been shown that both the RF and RI forms can activate MDA5 upon transfection (Feng et al., 2012; Triantafilou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RF and RI forms could be processed by RNases within the cell following transfection or infection, releasing the L antisense fragment that associates with LGP2.
source: It is conceivable that RF and RI forms could be processed by RNases within the cell following transfection or infection, releasing the L antisense fragment that associates with LGP2.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: The L region antisense fragment enriched in the LGP2 IP may be only one of several agonists generated upon EMCV replication.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that the L region antisense fragment enriched in our IP is only one of several agonists generated upon EMCV replication and that the RF and RI forms constitute a different set of agonists that do not strongly associate with LGP2 and have therefore been missed in our approach.
evidence: This is speculation about possible additional agonists.

claim: EMCVΔL viruses still possess the ability to induce low levels of IFN and IFIT-1.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with our data, which show that EMCVΔL viruses still possess the ability to induce low levels of IFN and IFIT-1 (Figures 6 and 7) and generate stimulatory RNA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: There exists at least one additional stimulatory RNA species beside the L region antisense fragment.
source: Such data suggest the existence of at least one additional stimulatory RNA species beside the L region antisense fragment and help explain why EMCVΔL is an attenuated strain: the additional stimulatory RNA means that it cannot fully evade innate immune detection while the lack of the L protein means that it cannot suppress the consequences of detection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EMCVΔL still induces some IFN response.

claim: This is the first study to identify an MDA5 agonist bound to LGP2 in infected cells.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to identify an MDA5 agonist bound to LGP2 in infected cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Picornaviruses constitute a large family of viruses that encompasses many human and animal pathogens including some of economical or medical importance including Poliovirus, Coxsackievirus, Rhinovirus, and EMCV.
source: Picornaviruses constitute a large family of viruses that encompasses many human and animal pathogens including some of economical or medical importance including Poliovirus, Coxsackievirus, Rhinovirus, and EMCV (Tuthill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The L regions of picornaviruses can show wide variation.
source: The L regions of picornaviruses can show wide variation and it will be interesting to determine to what extent L region RNA or other small RNAs can act as MDA5 agonists across picornavirus genera.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact and sets up future research directions.
